blocks.title: What this section is, and is not
text: RCF English is an English site, so this section is **deliberately small**. We do not teach Science or Maths, and we copy nobody's material. We point you to the official English medium resources, and then teach the part that is genuinely an English problem: understanding what a question asks, and writing an answer that earns the mark.
**Every link was opened and checked.** They sit on other people's websites and can change without notice. If one stops working, tell us and we will fix it.

blocks.heading: Why English medium is difficult, and what actually fixes it
text: A pupil who could explain photosynthesis perfectly in Sinhala or Tamil can lose the mark in English for three reasons, and none of them is Science.

**The question word is misread.** *Describe* and *explain* are not the same instruction, and a pupil who describes when the paper says explain has answered a different question. **The sentence collapses under the technical words.** The vocabulary is known, but the grammar holding it together is not. **The answer is right but unreadable.** No units, no labels, no order.
All three are language problems with language solutions, and they are the fastest marks a teacher can win back.

blocks.heading: Sentences that carry an answer
intro: Most answers in either subject use a handful of sentence shapes. Give pupils these and they stop translating sentence by sentence from their first language.
rows: *The bulb lights because the circuit is complete.*
*The pressure falls, so the volume increases.*
*The fuse prevents the wire from overheating.*
Say what a thing is made of
*An atom consists of a nucleus and electrons.*
*As the temperature rises, the resistance increases.*
*First the seed absorbs water, then the root appears.*
*If the triangle is equilateral, then all angles are 60°.*

blocks.heading: Mistakes that cost marks in English medium answers

items.q: Writing the unit only at the end, or not at all
a: A number without a unit is not an answer in Science or Maths. Write the unit every time it appears, including in the working, and use the standard form: 12 cm², 5 m/s, 250 g. Teach pupils to check the units before they check the arithmetic.

items.q: Using the everyday word instead of the technical one
a: *Melt*, *dissolve* and *evaporate* are three different things, and pupils use them for each other because in conversation they feel the same. The same happens with *weight* and *mass*, *heat* and *temperature*, *speed* and *velocity*. Put the pair on the board together and make pupils say a sentence with each.

items.q: Answering in the first language and translating word by word
a: This produces sentences that are grammatically strange and often lose the point. It is faster to teach the sentence shapes above than to correct translated sentences one at a time.

items.q: Describing when the question says explain
a: The most expensive mistake on the paper. If the word *because* does not appear in an answer to an *explain* question, the answer is very likely incomplete.

items.q: Diagram labels in the first language, or no labels
a: Labels are marks. Pupils should practise labelling the same standard diagrams in English until it is automatic: the digestive system, a plant cell, a circuit, the parts of a flower, a ray diagram, a triangle with its vertices named.

items.q: Long sentences where three short ones were wanted
a: Science and maths English is short and plain. One idea, one sentence. A pupil who writes three short correct sentences scores better than one who writes a long sentence that falls apart in the middle.

blocks.title: For the teacher: five minutes at the start of a lesson
text: **Word pair of the day.** Put up two words pupils confuse (*mass* and *weight*) and make each pupil say one sentence with each.
**Read the question aloud.** Before pupils answer, ask what the instruction word is and what shape of answer it wants. Half the class will have been about to answer the wrong question.
**Label it in English.** Keep one diagram on the board through the week and have a different pupil label it each day.
**Say the number with its unit.** Insist that every answer spoken aloud includes the unit. It transfers to the written paper faster than any correction.

blocks.heading: What the maths question word is telling you to do
intro: Each instruction asks for a different amount of working. A pupil who writes the answer alone where the paper said *show that* has thrown away most of the marks.
rows: The working, then the answer with its unit.
Every step, ending exactly at the value you were given.
*Since a = 2 and b = 3, a + b = 5, as required.*
A reason beside each step, ending in the statement asked for.
The value or values of the unknown.
One expression, as short as it will go. No equals-sign chain to a number.
A single number, with its unit if it has one.
The expression written as a product of brackets.
A drawing made with compasses and a straight edge, arcs left showing.
A construction with its arcs still visible.
An accurate drawing, then the measurement written with its unit.
Use the answer you just found. Do not start again.
A rounded value, with the rounding shown.

blocks.heading: Turning an English word problem into a sum
intro: Word problems are a reading test as much as a maths test. These are the phrases that decide the operation, and the ones pupils reverse most often.
rows: *8 more than x* is x + 8, not 8 + x reversed in meaning
*5 less than x* is x − 5, **not** 5 − x. Pupils reverse this constantly.
Take the smaller from the larger unless the question says otherwise
*half of x* is x ÷ 2, written x/2
Multiply or divide, by the rate
*60 km per hour* for 3 hours is 60 × 3
Name the unknown before you start
Always write this line down; it earns marks
Even or odd consecutive numbers go up in twos

blocks.heading: Saying and writing maths in English

items.q: How do I read these aloud?
a: Pupils who cannot say it often cannot write it either.
bullets: **x²** - x squared. **x³** - x cubed. **x⁴** - x to the power of four
**√9** - the square root of nine
**3/4** - three quarters, or three over four in an expression
**2 : 3** - the ratio two to three
**12 ÷ 4** - twelve divided by four
**∠ABC** - angle A B C
**≈** - is approximately equal to. **≥** - is greater than or equal to
**(x + 2)(x + 3)** - bracket x plus two, bracket x plus three

items.q: The lines that earn method marks
a: Marks are given for the working, not only the answer. These lines cost seconds and are worth marks.
bullets: *Let x be the number of books.*
*Let the two angles be x and 2x.*
*Therefore x = 7.*
*Hence the perimeter is 24 cm.*
Always finish with the unit: cm, cm², kg, rupees

items.q: Words pupils mix up in maths
a: Teach each pair together, in one sentence each.
bullets: **Area** and **perimeter** - one is the space inside, one is the distance around
**Volume** and **capacity** - the space a solid takes up, and how much it holds
**Numerator** and **denominator** - top and bottom of a fraction
**Factor** and **multiple** - 3 is a factor of 12; 12 is a multiple of 3
**Odd** and **even**; **prime** and **composite**
**Equation** and **expression** - an equation has an equals sign

blocks.heading: What the science question word is telling you to do
intro: Each instruction asks for a different shape of answer. Learn these and a pupil stops writing the wrong kind of answer to a question they actually understood.
rows: One fact. No reason, no sentence needed.
Several facts, one after another. Still no reasons.
*The three states are solid, liquid and gas.*
What happens, in order. Still no reasons.
*The water is heated. Bubbles form at the base, then rise ...*
The reason. This is where *because* belongs.
*The warm water rises because it is less dense.*
Both things in one sentence, with a linking word.
*Copper conducts heat well, whereas plastic does not.*
A complete sentence naming the thing and its key feature.
*Density is the mass of one unit of volume of a substance.*
A diagram with words on it. No sentence needed.
A ruled diagram, each part named in English.
A sensible answer using what you know, even if not in the book.
*The plant may have received too little light.*

blocks.heading: Writing up an experiment
intro: The write-up has the same five parts every time, and each part has its own grammar. The method is written in the **passive**: nobody's name appears in it.
rows: One sentence saying what you are finding out.
*To find out how temperature affects the rate of dissolving.*
The steps, in order, in the passive and the past tense.
*The water **was heated** to 40 °C. The salt **was added** and the time **was recorded**.*
What you saw or measured. A table if there are numbers.
What it shows, linked back to the aim.
*Therefore the salt dissolves faster at a higher temperature.*

items.q: Pairs to teach together, never apart
a: Each pair feels the same in conversation and means something different in Science. Put both on the board and make pupils say one sentence with each.
bullets: **Mass** and **weight** - how much matter, and the pull of gravity on it
**Heat** and **temperature** - the energy, and how hot something is
**Melt**, **dissolve** and **evaporate** - three different changes
**Speed** and **velocity** - velocity has a direction
**Transparent**, **translucent** and **opaque**
**Solute**, **solvent** and **solution**
**Reflection** and **refraction** - bouncing back, and bending
**Respiration** and **breathing** - the reaction in the cell, and moving air

items.q: Diagrams worth labelling in English until it is automatic
a: Labels are marks, and they are the easiest marks on the paper to practise.
bullets: The human digestive system and the heart
A plant cell and an animal cell
The parts of a flower
A simple electrical circuit, with its symbols
A ray diagram through a lens or prism
The apparatus for a common experiment: filtration, distillation

items.q: Units, and where marks are lost
a: A number without a unit is not an answer. Write the unit every time, including in the working.
bullets: Length **cm, m, km**; mass **g, kg**; time **s, min**
Area **cm²**; volume **cm³**; capacity **ml, l**
Temperature **°C**; force **N**; energy **J**; power **W**
Speed **m/s**; density **g/cm³**
